citation.authors: APT / dpkg / debconf developers (Debian); Debian snapshot team; Canonical
citation.title: apt-get(8), apt(8), dpkg(1), dpkg-query(1), debconf(7), sources.list(5); snapshot.debian.org; Ubuntu Snapshot Service

claims.planned: apt-get update resynchronizes package index files from sources; install pkg=version pins a version; apt is the interactive front-end whose CLI 'may change' - scripts should use apt-get (exact wording from apt(8))
claims.finding: All three confirmed verbatim. apt(8) exact wording: the apt command line 'is designed as an end-user tool and it may change behavior between versions'; 'you should prefer using these commands [apt-get, apt-cache] ... in your scripts as they keep backward compatibility as much as possible.' Version selection: package name followed by '=' and the version.
claims.quote: The apt(8) commandline is designed as an end-user tool and it may change behavior between versions. While it tries not to break backward compatibility this is not guaranteed either if a change seems beneficial for interactive use.
claims.location: apt(8) > SCRIPT USAGE AND DIFFERENCES FROM OTHER APT TOOLS

claims.planned: -y, --no-install-recommends, DEBIAN_FRONTEND=noninteractive (debconf(7)) to avoid interactive prompts hanging a build/agent
claims.finding: -y/--yes/--assume-yes: 'Automatic yes to prompts ... run non-interactively' but apt-get still ABORTS on 'undesirable' situations (held package change, unauthenticated package, removing an essential package). --no-install-recommends: 'Do not consider recommended packages as a dependency for installing'. debconf(7): the noninteractive frontend 'never interacts with you at all, and makes the default answers be used for all questions'; DEBIAN_FRONTEND is 'Used to temporarily change the frontend debconf uses'. -y alone does NOT silence debconf questions (e.g. tzdata) - that is what DEBIAN_FRONTEND=noninteractive is for. Docker's Dockerfile reference warns against baking it in with ENV (use per-command or ARG).
claims.quote: noninteractive This is the anti-frontend. It never interacts with you at all, and makes the default answers be used for all questions. It might mail error messages to root, but that's it; otherwise it is completely silent and unobtrusive, a perfect frontend for automatic installs.

claims.planned: dpkg -l lists installed packages and versions; dpkg -S path finds owning package; dpkg -L lists files; /var/lib/dpkg/status; dpkg lock (/var/lib/dpkg/lock-frontend) - the 'Could not get lock' error when two apt processes run
claims.finding: dpkg(1): -l 'List packages matching given pattern', -s 'Report status of specified package', -L 'List files installed to your system from package-name', -S 'Search for a filename from installed packages' (all forwarded to dpkg-query). /var/lib/dpkg/status: 'Statuses of available packages ... whether it is installed or not'. The bookworm dpkg(1) page does not name the lock-frontend file path; it documents the mechanism via DPKG_FRONTEND_LOCKED ('frontend lock (since dpkg 1.19.1)'). The file path and the exact error were verified by EXECUTION: /var/lib/dpkg/lock-frontend exists in ubuntu:24.04, and a second concurrent apt-get prints 'E: Could not get lock /var/lib/dpkg/lock-frontend. It is held by process 133 (apt-get)' and exits 100.
claims.quote:
$ docker run --rm --name lt-R5-lock ubuntu:24.04 bash -c 'apt-get update -q >/dev/null 2>&1; (apt-get install -y -q curl >/dev/null 2>&1 &); sleep 2; apt-get install -y wget; echo "exit=$?"'
E: Could not get lock /var/lib/dpkg/lock-frontend. It is held by process 133 (apt-get)
E: Unable to acquire the dpkg frontend lock (/var/lib/dpkg/lock-frontend), is another process using it?
exit=100
claims.location: executed ubuntu:24.04 (apt 2.8.3); man text at dpkg(1) > dpkg-query actions / FILES / ENVIRONMENT

claims.planned: Distribution repos only carry the CURRENT version of a package in a release pocket: an old pinned version can disappear, breaking rebuilds -> snapshot.debian.org 'wayback machine' for the archive; snapshot.ubuntu.com for Ubuntu 23.10+ with APT snapshot option
claims.finding: (a) 'Only the current version is carried' is NOT stated in any fetched man page or snapshot page - it is unverifiable as a quoted rule, but was demonstrated by EXECUTION: in ubuntu:24.04 on 2026-09-20 `apt-cache madison curl` offered only 8.5.0-2ubuntu10.13 (noble-updates/-security) and 8.5.0-2ubuntu10 (release pocket); pinning an intermediate version that once existed fails with "E: Version '8.5.0-2ubuntu10.4' for 'curl' was not found" (exit 100). Pinning the still-listed release-pocket version also failed, on dependencies ('curl : Depends: libcurl4t64 (= 8.5.0-2ubuntu10) but 8.5.0-2ubuntu10.13 is to be installed') - pins must cover the dependency set. (b) snapshot.debian.org: 'wayback machine' wording confirmed verbatim; imports 'from 2005 until the present'; URL form https://snapshot.debian.org/archive/debian/<yyyymmddThhmmssZ>/; old snapshots need [check-valid-until=no]. (c) CORRECTION on Ubuntu details: snapshots exist for dates after 1 March 2023; supported in Ubuntu 23.10 onwards PLUS updated 20.04 LTS (apt 2.0.10) and 22.04 LTS (apt 2.4.11); on 24.04+ apt enables it AUTOMATICALLY for the official repos (no sources edit), and it is used with `--snapshot <ID>` / `-S <ID>` or APT::Snapshot; on 23.10 and earlier you add [snapshot=yes]. Retention promise is only 'at least 2 years in the past'. The ubuntu.com blog URL in sources.json returns 404; snapshot.ubuntu.com itself is the primary source.
claims.quote: The snapshot archive is a wayback machine that allows access to old packages based on dates and version numbers. It consists of all past and current packages the Debian archive provides.
claims.location: snapshot.debian.org front page (intro); snapshot.ubuntu.com 'Ubuntu Snapshot Service'

claims.planned: Official Docker images strip apt lists (/var/lib/apt/lists) so apt-get install fails before apt-get update - verify by running
claims.finding: Verified by execution in both ubuntu:24.04 and debian:bookworm-slim: /var/lib/apt/lists is empty and install fails with 'E: Unable to locate package curl', exit status 100. (Docker's best-practices page documents the rm -rf /var/lib/apt/lists/* convention and that official Debian/Ubuntu images auto-run apt-get clean.)
claims.quote:
$ docker run --rm ubuntu:24.04 bash -c 'ls -la /var/lib/apt/lists/; apt-get install -y curl; echo "exit=$?"'
total 8
drwxr-xr-x 2 root root 4096 Sep 11 02:12 .
drwxr-xr-x 5 root root 4096 Sep 11 02:12 ..
Reading package lists...
Building dependency tree...
Reading state information...
E: Unable to locate package curl
exit=100
claims.location: executed ubuntu:24.04 (identical error and exit=100 in debian:bookworm-slim)

extra_findings.finding: apt-get update definition (exact).
extra_findings.quote: update is used to resynchronize the package index files from their sources. The indexes of available packages are fetched from the location(s) specified in /etc/apt/sources.list. [...] An update should always be performed before an upgrade or dist-upgrade.

extra_findings.finding: Version selection (exact).
extra_findings.quote: A specific version of a package can be selected for installation by following the package name with an equals and the version of the package to select. This will cause that version to be located and selected for install.

extra_findings.finding: apt-get's role.
extra_findings.quote: apt-get is the command-line tool for handling packages, and may be considered the user's "back-end" to other tools using the APT library.

extra_findings.finding: apt(8) second paragraph: prefer apt-get/apt-cache in scripts.
extra_findings.quote: All features of apt(8) are available in dedicated APT tools like apt-get(8) and apt-cache(8) as well. [...] So you should prefer using these commands (potentially with some additional options enabled) in your scripts as they keep backward compatibility as much as possible.
extra_findings.location: apt(8) > SCRIPT USAGE AND DIFFERENCES FROM OTHER APT TOOLS

extra_findings.finding: apt(8) description.
extra_findings.quote: apt provides a high-level commandline interface for the package management system. It is intended as an end user interface and enables some options better suited for interactive usage by default

extra_findings.finding: -y exact text and its limits.
extra_findings.quote: Automatic yes to prompts; assume "yes" as answer to all prompts and run non-interactively. If an undesirable situation, such as changing a held package, trying to install an unauthenticated package or removing an essential package occurs then apt-get will abort.

extra_findings.finding: --no-install-recommends.
extra_findings.quote: Do not consider recommended packages as a dependency for installing. Configuration Item: APT::Install-Recommends.

extra_findings.finding: -q / -qq: -qq implies -y and the man page warns against it.
extra_findings.quote: Note that quiet level 2 implies -y; you should never use -qq without a no-action modifier such as -d, --print-uris or -s as APT may decide to do something you did not expect.

extra_findings.finding: apt-get clean.
extra_findings.quote: clean clears out the local repository of retrieved package files. It removes everything but the lock file from /var/cache/apt/archives/ and /var/cache/apt/archives/partial/.

extra_findings.finding: --allow-downgrades is flagged dangerous (needed when pinning below an installed version).
extra_findings.quote: This is a dangerous option that will cause apt to continue without prompting if it is doing downgrades. It should not be used except in very special situations.

extra_findings.finding: dpkg-query -l details.
extra_findings.quote: List all known packages matching one or more patterns [...] If no package-name-pattern is given, list all packages in /var/lib/dpkg/status, excluding the ones marked as not-installed [...] The first three columns of the output show the desired action, the package status, and errors, in that order.

extra_findings.finding: dpkg-query -S.
extra_findings.quote: Search for packages that own files corresponding to the given patterns.

extra_findings.finding: dpkg status file.
extra_findings.quote: /var/lib/dpkg/status Statuses of available packages. This file contains information about whether a package is marked for removing or not, whether it is installed or not, etc.

extra_findings.finding: Frontend lock env var.
extra_findings.quote: DPKG_FRONTEND_LOCKED Set by a package manager frontend to notify dpkg that it should not acquire the frontend lock (since dpkg 1.19.1).

extra_findings.finding: snapshot.debian.org usage: sources.list lines, date formats, nearest-earlier semantics.
extra_findings.quote: deb https://snapshot.debian.org/archive/debian/20091004T111800Z/ lenny main [...] Valid date formats are yyyymmddThhmmssZ or simply yyyymmdd. If there is no import at the exact time you specified you will get the latest available timestamp which is before the time you specified.

extra_findings.finding: snapshot.debian.org and expired Release files.
extra_findings.quote: To access snapshots of suites using Valid-Until that are older than a dozen days, it is necessary to ignore the Valid-Until header within Release files, in order to prevent apt from disregarding snapshot entries ("Release file expired"). [...] deb [check-valid-until=no] https://snapshot.debian.org/archive/debian/20091004T111800Z/ lenny main

extra_findings.finding: snapshot.debian.org purpose and coverage; https needs ca-certificates (http also works).
extra_findings.quote: It provides a valuable resource for tracking down when regressions were introduced, or for providing a specific environment that a particular application may require to run. [...] we have imports for the main Debian archive [...] from 2005 until the present.

extra_findings.finding: Ubuntu snapshot service: definition, start date, use cases.
extra_findings.quote: The Ubuntu snapshot service makes it possible to see and use the Ubuntu archive as it was at any specified date and time. Snapshots of the Ubuntu archive are available for any date and time after 1 March 2023.

extra_findings.finding: Ubuntu snapshot support matrix + retention.
extra_findings.quote: Snapshots are supported in Ubuntu 23.10 onwards, plus on updated installations of Ubuntu 20.04 LTS (apt 2.0.10) and Ubuntu 22.04 LTS (apt 2.4.11). We intend to ensure snapshots are available for dates up to at least 2 years in the past, which we may extend if there is demand.

extra_findings.finding: Ubuntu 24.04 quick start (exact command).
extra_findings.quote: apt install hello --update --snapshot 20240301T030400Z

extra_findings.finding: Ubuntu 24.04 auto-detects snapshot support; 23.10 and earlier need [snapshot=yes].
extra_findings.quote: The apt included in Ubuntu 24.04 and later automatically detects when snapshots are supported for a repository (any repository with a Snapshots: directive in the Release file). This includes the official Ubuntu repositories, so snapshots for these will be enabled by default.
extra_findings.location: snapshot.ubuntu.com > Enable snapshot service on configured repositories

extra_findings.finding: Snapshot ID format; system-wide pin via apt.conf; per-source via 'Snapshot: <ID>' (deb822) or [snapshot=<ID>].
extra_findings.quote: The Snapshot ID will be the desired date and UTC time in the YYYYMMDDTHHMMSSZ format [...] echo 'APT::Snapshot "20240301T030400Z";' | sudo tee /etc/apt/apt.conf.d/50snapshot
extra_findings.location: snapshot.ubuntu.com > Use a Snapshot ID with apt Commands

extra_findings.finding: Ubuntu noble apt-get(8) documents -S/--snapshot (NOT present in the Debian bookworm apt-get(8)).
extra_findings.quote: -S, --snapshot This option controls the snapshot chosen for archives with Snapshot: enable in the source entry. For example, -S 20220102T030405Z selects a snapshot from January 2nd, 2022 at 03:04:05 UTC. Configuration Item: APT::Snapshot

extra_findings.finding: Ubuntu noble sources.list(5) Snapshot option (the Debian bookworm sources.list(5) has no snapshot option at all).
extra_findings.quote: Snapshot (snapshot) allows selecting an earlier version of the archive from the snapshot service. Supported values are: enable to allow selecting a snapshot with the --snapshot option, or a snapshot ID to select a specific snapshot.

extra_findings.finding: Docker's convention for apt lists in images.
extra_findings.quote: when you clean up the apt cache by removing `/var/lib/apt/lists` it reduces the image size, since the apt cache isn't stored in a layer. [...] Official Debian and Ubuntu images automatically run `apt-get clean`, so explicit invocation is not required.

teaching_notes: access=partial only because https://ubuntu.com/blog/ubuntu-snapshot-service returned 404; everything needed is on snapshot.ubuntu.com. The apt(8) 'may change behavior between versions ... prefer these commands in your scripts' wording is confirmed verbatim - good ammunition for 'agents and Dockerfiles should call apt-get'. Corrections/surprises: (1) no primary source states the folklore rule 'repos carry only the current version'; teach it from the executed madison output + the exact "Version ... was not found" error; (2) pinning a single package is not enough - dependencies are version-locked (libcurl4t64), so a pin list must be closed over dependencies or use a snapshot; (3) Ubuntu snapshots: on 24.04 they are ON by default for official repos and used via --snapshot/-S; coverage starts 1 March 2023 and Canonical only promises ~2 years retention - so it is not a permanent archive, unlike snapshot.debian.org (2005-present); (4) stock ubuntu:24.04 cannot use the HTTPS snapshot server until ca-certificates is installed (chicken-and-egg worth a callout); (5) the --snapshot option and sources.list Snapshot field are Ubuntu-noble apt features and are absent from Debian bookworm's man pages; (6) -y does not suppress debconf prompts, and -qq implies -y with a man-page warning; (7) exit status for all these apt failures is 100. Architecture caveat: all executed output is arm64 (ports.ubuntu.com); amd64 hosts use archive.ubuntu.com/security.ubuntu.com.
